title: The King's Indian Defence
standfirst: Every principle you've learned so far says don't let your opponent take the whole centre. The King's Indian breaks that rule deliberately — and it works.

steps.title: Breaking the rule on purpose
body: So far the message has been simple: fight for the centre. The King's Indian lets White build the biggest centre he likes, then attacks it with pieces from a distance.
This is a hypermodern opening. The rule isn't wrong — it's that a big centre is also a big target.

steps.title: Control d5 with a piece
body: Not …d5. Black stops White's e-pawn from advancing using a piece rather than a pawn — the hypermodern idea in a single move.

steps.title: Take more
body: White grabs a second big centre pawn. Black is going to let him.

steps.title: Preparing the fianchetto
body: The little pawn move that names the system. It clears g7 for the bishop, which will spend the game on the long diagonal aimed at White's centre.

steps.title: Natural development
body: White builds calmly, controlling d5 and e4.

steps.title: The fianchettoed bishop
body: There it is, on the a1–h8 diagonal, pointing at d4 and beyond. It may be blocked for twenty moves — and then the centre opens and it becomes the strongest piece on the board.

steps.title: The full centre, accepted
body: White now has pawns on c4, d4 and e4 — everything the earlier studies said to aim for. By classical standards White is simply better.
The King's Indian player is entirely content. A big centre must be defended, and it can be attacked.

steps.title: A small move with a big future
body: Modest, but it does two things: it stops e4–e5 from steamrolling the position, and it prepares the pawn break that this whole opening exists for.

steps.title: Solid development
body: White develops naturally and guards e5.

steps.title: Castle first, fight later
body: Black tucks the king away behind the fianchetto — a famously safe structure — before starting anything. Even in sharp openings, king safety comes first.

steps.title: The Classical setup
body: White completes his development modestly, ready to castle. Everything is about to become concrete.

steps.title: The strike the whole opening was built for
body: Here it is. Black finally hits the centre, and every earlier move now makes sense: …d6 supported this pawn, …Bg7 and …Nf6 are already aimed at the squares that open up.

White usually plays d4–d5, locking the centre. Then the game becomes a famous race: Black storms the kingside with …f5, …f4 and …g5, White breaks through on the queenside with c4–c5. Whoever gets there first wins — which is exactly why people love this opening.
